seed_commits.message:
chore: initial project scaffold

FastAPI service, Postgres in compose and the CI skeleton. No application
code yet.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Delgado <rosa.delgado@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(db): tenants, api keys and the four fact tables

tenant_id is denormalised onto every fact table rather than inferred through
a join. order_items could reach its tenant through orders, but then a query
touching order_items alone would have nothing to filter on.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Delgado <rosa.delgado@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(tenancy): API-key authentication and the request tenant context

Keys are stored as SHA-256 and looked up by hash, so there is no comparison
to time and a dump of the table yields no working credential. The tenant
itself travels in a ContextVar: it is needed by the policy, the executor and
the audit logger, and a parameter threaded through six layers is one that
will eventually be passed wrongly by one of them.
seed_commits.author: Yusuf Demir <yusuf.demir@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(nl2sql): catalog, prompt assembly and the recorded model client

The model is a fixture, not an API call. Generations are keyed by
sha256(model|system|prompt) and a miss is an error -- a suite that quietly
reaches the internet fails differently on every machine and costs money to
run.

Consequence worth knowing: the prompt embeds the schema section, so editing
the catalog moves every cassette key at once.
seed_commits.author: Yusuf Demir <yusuf.demir@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(policy): constrain generated SQL to the asking tenant

The rewrite walks query scopes rather than tables. A statement is a tree of
scopes -- the outer select, each CTE body, each derived table, each branch of
a set operation -- and every one can reference a base table independently.
Scoping only the outermost one produces a query that is valid, returns
plausible rows, and reads the whole table.

Fails closed throughout: an unresolvable reference raises rather than being
skipped, and the walk asserts at the end that every scoped table it read
actually received a predicate.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Delgado <rosa.delgado@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(nl2sql): executor, audit trail and the request pipeline

The tenant is bound as a query parameter, never formatted into SQL, which is
why there is no escaping helper in this codebase. Audit records hold the SQL
that ran rather than the SQL that was generated, and are written on the
rejection path too -- a trail of successes describes a service where nobody
has ever tried anything.
seed_commits.author: Marcus Webb <marcus.webb@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(api): ask, schema and audit endpoints, plus the CLI

No endpoint takes a tenant parameter. It comes from the API key and from
nowhere else -- no header a client can set, no override for internal callers.

/v1/schema returns names only. Row counts and sample values are things people
ask for to help the model, and both turn it into a way to read another
tenant's data one statistic at a time.
seed_commits.author: Marcus Webb <marcus.webb@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(db): restrict the application role and enable row-level security

Postgres exempts a table's owner from its RLS policies unless the table is
declared FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. A service connecting as the owner has RLS
enabled and inert: the policies exist, \d lists them, and they filter
nothing.

So migrations run as the owner, the app runs as sqlgenie_app which owns
nothing, and all four fact tables force RLS anyway. Two mechanisms for one
property, because the failure mode is invisible.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Delgado <rosa.delgado@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(fixtures): deterministic two-tenant development data

Both tenants get the same customer names, SKUs, order ids and totals. Only
tenant_id differs.

That is deliberate. With distinguishable fixtures a cross-tenant leak returns
rows that look sensible, so a test passes for the wrong reason and whoever
wrote it moves on. Identical data gives a leak exactly one signature: the row
count doubles.
seed_commits.author: Yusuf Demir <yusuf.demir@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
test: cover the policy, the cassette set and cross-tenant isolation

The security suite is split three ways on purpose: the rewriter with no
database, the database executing deliberately unscoped SQL, and the whole
pipeline. Defence in depth means an end-to-end assertion passes if either
layer works, so a suite of only end-to-end tests would stay green with the
rewriter completely broken.

The adversarial corpus includes one legitimate cross-tenant question that
must be allowed. Without it, refusing everything would pass the file.
seed_commits.author: Marcus Webb <marcus.webb@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
ci: run the suite, the adversarial corpus and a smoke question

ci/run_ci.sh mirrors the workflow so the same steps can be run locally. The
policy and cassette tests run first with the database and the network both
pointed at dead ports, which is how a stray connection in what is supposed to
be a pure rewrite gets caught here rather than in production.
seed_commits.author: Rosa Delgado <rosa.delgado@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
feat(prompt): richer prompt template for comparative questions

Year-over-year questions were producing a subquery per metric and getting the
numbers wrong when the two sides had different row counts. The prompt now
asks for each side as a named common table expression joined in the final
select, which keeps each side's filters explicit.

Re-recorded the affected cassettes.
seed_commits.author: Yusuf Demir <yusuf.demir@example.com>

seed_commits.message:
perf: measure query cost in work rather than milliseconds

Statements sent, catalog lookups made, rows examined. A wall-clock number on
a laptop running Docker describes the laptop; a statement count is identical
on every machine.
seed_commits.author: Marcus Webb <marcus.webb@example.com>
